title: Cutting migration risks Australia’s middle-power clout
gist: Roggeveen argues that cuts to migration favoured by Australia's three most popular political entities will shrink economic scale and risk reducing Australia from middle power to small power as the region becomes more volatile.

insights.claim: Australia's Labor, the Liberal-Nationals Coalition and One Nation all now favour lower immigration, with dramatic cuts proposed by the Coalition and One Nation.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Political consensus points to lower population growth and weaker aggregate demand.

insights.claim: Severe migration cuts will erode Australia's national power and economic scale, and restrict ties with Asia since Asians are a majority of the migrant intake.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Slower population growth reduces aggregate GDP and regional links.
insights.locator: Australia is flirting with a retreat

insights.claim: Aggregate wealth, not per capita wealth, determines how national wealth converts to military capability and global rank; with 10 million rather than 28 million Australians the economy would be much smaller.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Scale matters for strategic weight even if per capita income is unaffected.

insights.claim: Great powers make and enforce rules, small powers obey them, and middle powers lack strength to make rules but can resist having them imposed.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Useful lens for assessing a country's coercion exposure.
insights.quote: Middle powers have too little strength to make the rules but enough strength to resist having the rules imposed upon them.
insights.locator: We can divide the world’s 193 UN member states

insights.claim: The 2018 exclusion of Huawei from Australian mobile infrastructure illustrates what a middle power can do while absorbing blowback, which a small power cannot.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Shrinking national scale would reduce Australia's ability to take such decisions against China.

insights.claim: With China rising, America declining and Indonesia soon to have greater national power than Australia, migration policy may decide whether Australia stays a middle power or becomes a small power that pre-emptively accedes to great-power demands.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Australia faces gradual strategic deference risk rather than overt coercion.
